newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Hope seen for end to worst forms of child labour.
newsitem.headline: Hope seen for end to worst forms of child labour.

text.p: Sweeping political and economic changes around the world are bringing real hope of an end to the worst forms of child exploitation, delegates told an international conference on child labour on Wednesday.
"There has been a radical change in attitudes towards the problem," Michel Hansenne, director-general of the International Labour Office (ILO), told the two-day meeting in Amsterdam.
"We are convinced we can now make a decisive breakthrough in the struggle against child labour."

The ILO estimates there are as many as 250 million child labourers in the developing world, many working under intolerable conditions -- as slaves, forced labourers, prostitutes, or in surroundings which damage their health.

But Hansenne said such labour was no longer internationally accepted as an inevitable consequence of underdevelopment or poverty and the changing world economy was bringing new hope of stopping extreme exploitation.

"The ongoing globalisation of the economy and trade has a beneficial impact on growth and employment, which will provide developing countries with greater resources to reduce the economic necessity of child labour," he said.
Concerted action on child labour has long been complicated by a political dimension to the debate.
Developing nations are deeply suspicious of Western interference in the area of workers rights, fearing this will undermine their main comparative advantage in world trade -- cheap labour.
Some contend that Western nations are using the issue to disguise nascent protectionism and gain unfair trade advantages.
While welcoming the intentions of the conference, Indian Labour Minister M.Arunachalam, said Western countries needed to understand and empathise with the plight of developing nations.

"Any attempts to link the issue of working children with international trade and to use it to impose trade sanctions, directly or indirectly, on countries where child labour exists, are likely to prove counterproductive and are bound to jeopardise the welfare of these very children," he said.
In India, labour ministry officials say 18 million children are at work rather than at school, while children's-rights activists put the figure at around 55 million.
In December, the country said it had taken 150,000 child labourers out of hazardous industries under a plan to eliminate children from such jobs by 2002.
In contrast, German Labour Minister Norbert Blum said he favoured any measures, including boycotts, which would crack down on intolerable forms of exploitation.

"To call these practices 'child labour' is far too mild," he said. "Bonded labour and debt bondage is slavery. Child prostitution is a crime, it can be murder. You can kill a person's mind and soul as surely as their body."
"The people who take part in these things are swine and they must be stopped."

A background report prepared for the conference says tens of millions of child labourers in South Asia are kept in slavery or under forced labour systems such as debt bondage, where children work to pay off a family obligation.
The report said sexual exploitation of children was increasing and noted the effects.
"Case studies reveal a trauma so deep that many such children are unable to return to a normal life. Many others die before adulthood," it says.
Hansenne proposed a new ILO convention be established expressly forbidding all extreme forms of child labour in any of the organisation's 174 member states.
The Amsterdam conference would provide the framework for initial discussions on the new document, which would hopefully be introduced in 1999, he said.

However, no ban could work in the absence of social aid to developing countries and some form of monitoring mechanism to ensure compliance, Conference Chairman Ad Melkert, Dutch social affairs minister, said.
"We must simultaneously offer alternatives to the children and their parents...and it would be a good thing if we could periodically evaluate what progress we have made," he said.
"We must break this vicious circle in which the working children of today are the illiterate workers of tomorrow, who put their own children to work the day after tomorrow."
